papers.title: PGC-1α Links Estrogen Receptor Signaling to Japanese Encephalitis Virus Replication in Neuronal cell
papers.abstract: Acute encephalitis due to the viral causative agents, such as Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV), remains a leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia, contributing to high mortality and long-term neurological sequelae. The host factors that modulate JEV replication are not well understood. In this study, we investigated the modulation of JEV infection by estrogen in vitro and in vivo. The results demonstrated that estrogen enhances JEV replication in neuronal cells via estrogen receptor alpha (ER) by modulating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1). Since JEV pathogenesis increases cellular production demands, it results in dysregulation of cellular homeostasis, whereas estrogen treatment helps keep cellular health in check. Also, the mouse model exhibited an increased viral burden with protective antibody titers in response to estrogen. Conclusively, this work highlights the mechanistic link of estrogen-driven mechanisms and identifies the ER-PGC-1-axis as a potential target for sex-specific therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Cardioselective β-blocker Therapy Resolves Staphylococcus aureus Toxin-Induced Innate Immunoparalysis
papers.abstract: During Staphylococcus aureus sepsis, the pore-forming -toxin (Hla) triggers lytic platelet death and provokes the release of catecholamines that modulate leukocyte effector function. The resulting surge in catecholaminergic action paralyzes host antimicrobial capacity by upregulating interleukin-10 (IL-10), profoundly suppressing the protective interferon (IFN) response to orchestrate innate immunoparalysis. Here, we deconvolute a multi-cellular regulatory pathway in the blood and highlight a pivotal immunological checkpoint, where pharmacological intervention with cardioselective {beta}-blockers uncouples the immunosuppressive cascade, restores host antimicrobial function, and significantly improves survival outcomes.

papers.title: Concentration-dependent inhibition of Streptococcus mutans metabolic activity by purified Croton lechleri latex (sangre de grado) in vitro
papers.abstract: Background. Chlorhexidine is the reference chemical antiplaque agent, but its adverse effects motivate the search for plant-derived alternatives. The proanthocyanidin-rich latex of Croton lechleri (sangre de grado) is a candidate, yet quantitative concentration-response data against Streptococcus mutans are scarce. Methods. In this exploratory in vitro study, ethanol-purified C. lechleri latex was tested at working concentrations of 3-100% v/v (final in-well concentrations 0.6-20% v/v) against S. mutans ATCC 25175 in a 96-well resazurin assay with dual-wavelength reading (570/600 nm) and correction for medium and latex color. Chlorhexidine 1% (0.2% in-well) was the positive control. Each condition was run in technical triplicate within a single experiment. Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA, Tukey's test with simultaneous 95% confidence intervals (CI) and four-parameter logistic regression. Results. Metabolic activity decreased monotonically with concentration, from 101.3 +/- 1.7% (vehicle) to 54.0 +/- 4.7% (12%), 15.5 +/- 4.0% (50%) and 8.6 +/- 7.7% (100%), compared with 3.1 +/- 2.8% for chlorhexidine (F(7,16) = 160.7, p < 0.001). The lowest concentration that differed from the vehicle was 6% (difference 17.6 percentage points, 95% CI 2.1-33.1). The estimated half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) was 12.3% v/v (95% CI 9.5-15.1). Differences from chlorhexidine at 50% and 100% were not statistically significant, but their confidence intervals were compatible with differences of up to 28 and 21 percentage points, respectively. Conclusions. Purified C. lechleri latex inhibited the metabolic activity of planktonic S. mutans in a concentration-dependent manner. These preliminary findings do not establish equivalence with chlorhexidine and warrant replication in independent experiments with chemically standardized extracts expressed in mg/mL, determination of MIC/MBC and biofilm models.

papers.title: Quantitative host-response mapping enables phenotypic profiling of viruses detected by virome sequencing
papers.abstract: Animal-derived viruses have repeatedly caused human outbreaks, motivating efforts to identify and characterize viruses circulating in animals. Virome sequencing has accelerated animal virus discovery, but phenotypic characterization remains difficult to scale. Although generated for viral detection, virome RNA-seq data also capture host transcriptional responses to infection. Here, we developed ViroChart, a comparative transcriptomic framework that quantifies activities across biological pathways and maps diverse mammalian host responses into a common, interpretable low-dimensional space. ViroChart enables clustering of infected samples by host response pattern and quantitative assessment of host response similarity between samples. In virome data sets from wild and farmed animals, some lung samples infected with poorly characterized betacoronaviruses showed host responses resembling those induced by viruses capable of causing fatal disease. ViroChart also revealed host-response heterogeneity in natural infections: among rats with zoonotic rodent-borne viruses, most showed weak responses, consistent with asymptomatic infection, but some showed pronounced inflammation characteristic of acute infection. ViroChart thus enables phenotypic characterization and prioritization of newly detected viruses by leveraging the same RNA-seq data from which their genomes were detected.

papers.title: Genomic and physiological characterization of Neobacillus ammoniipjilus sp. nov. reveals versatile inorganic nitrogen utilization and ammonia-mitigation potential
papers.abstract: A novel bacterial strain (KR4-4T), was isolated from soil in the Republic of Korea and subjected to polyphasic taxonomic and functional characterization. Phylogenetic analysis based on the 16S rRNA gene sequence placed strain KR4-4T within the genus Neobacillus. Phylogenomic analysis based on 92 bacterial core genes further supported its distinct taxonomic position. Average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values between KR4-4T and related Neobacillus type strains were 69.76-82.31% and 18.3-25.9%, respectively, supporting its recognition as a distinct species. Cells were Gram-stain-positive, non-motile, facultatively anaerobic rods, with growth occurring at 15-45 {degrees}C, pH 6.0-8.0, and 0-2.0% (w/v) NaCl. The major cellular fatty acids were iso-C15:0 and anteiso-C15:0, while the major polar lipids included diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylglycerol, and phosphatidylethanolamine. Genome analysis revealed genes associated with inorganic nitrogen transport, nitrate and nitrite reduction, and ammonium assimilation. In liquid culture, KR4-4T removed NH4+-N under aerobic conditions and was able to utilize ammonium, nitrate, and nitrite as individual nitrogen sources, with removal efficiencies of 86.5%, 69.35%, and 62.9%, respectively. The strain also contributed to the reduction of gaseous NH3 in a closed-flask assay. Together, these physiological and genomic characteristics indicate a versatile capacity for inorganic nitrogen utilization and transformation and suggest potential for further evaluation in biological ammonia-mitigation applications. Based on phylogenetic, genomic, phenotypic, and chemotaxonomic evidence, strain KR4-4T represents a novel species of the genus Neobacillus, for which the name Neobacillus ammoniiphilus sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is KR4-4T (= KACC 24003T = CCTCC AB 2025077T).

papers.title: A silent intergenic locus for efficient and versatile transgene expression in Plasmodium falciparum
papers.abstract: Genetically modified Plasmodium falciparum parasites expressing transgenes such as fluorescent markers are crucial tools for malaria research. However, current reporter lines often rely on integrated transgene constructs that disrupt the coding sequence of a native gene, potentially affecting progression in the life cycle of the tool parasite line. We identified six candidate Silent Intergenic Loci (SILs): putatively editable intergenic regions without transcriptional activity, where gene insertions occurred in P. falciparum after its divergence from Plasmodium berghei and Plasmodium vivax. We characterised the largest candidate SIL on chromosome 12, SIL12, by integration of a constitutively expressed cytosolic mScarlet reporter. The resulting PfRed12 parasites progressed normally throughout the life cycle, from asexual blood-stage replication to mosquito stages and subsequent liver infection. Importantly, they infected both Anopheles stephensi and Anopheles coluzzii mosquitoes. PfRed12 parasites displayed bright fluorescence in both blood and mosquito stages, making them well suited for live visualisation of parasite transmission. In addition, we used two CRISPR-Cas9 target sites in the mScarlet cassette, one of which we purposely added, to perform efficient re-editing of the transgene. As a proof of concept, we re-edited PfRed12 parasites and integrated an apicoplast metabolic bypass construct, an inducible gametocyte producer construct, and two mNeonGreen reporter constructs. Together, our findings demonstrate that SIL12 permits stable transgene expression without compromising parasite development throughout the life cycle. We established PfRed12 as a new reporter line to study blood- and mosquito-stage development and as a versatile parental line for further genetic engineering.

papers.title: Root exudates enhance the ecological fitness of a non-native PGPR and reshape rhizosphere microbiome assembly
papers.abstract: Root exudates play critical roles in rhizosphere microbiome assembly. Nevertheless, the molecular mechanisms by which plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) perceive these signals, adapt to the rhizosphere, and influence native microbial communities remain poorly understood. Here, using maize (Zea mays cv. Early Golden Bantam) and the rhizobacterium Priestia aryabhattai AB211, we took a multi-omics approach combining metabolomics, bacterial transcriptomics and proteomics, and rhizosphere metagenomics to elucidate the mechanism underlying this process. Maize root exudates were enriched in diverse carbon and nitrogen metabolites that promoted bacterial growth and induced extensive molecular reprogramming of pathways involved in nutrient acquisition, chemotaxis, motility, stress adaptation, and plant growth promotion, thereby enhancing rhizosphere competence. In field-conditioned soil, AB211 persisted as a core member of the maize rhizosphere microbiome, promoted early seedling growth, and reshaped microbial community composition and function. Root exudates-primed (RE-primed) AB211 further enhanced the enrichment of microbial functions associated with nutrient cycling, quorum sensing, plant growth promotion, and rhizosphere fitness, highlighting the role of root exudates in modulating the rhizosphere-adaptative potential of beneficial bacteria. These findings establish a mechanistic framework linking root exudates composition with PGPR adaptation and microbiome assembly, providing a foundation for engineering ecologically adapted microbial inoculants to improve crop productivity and sustainable agriculture.

papers.title: Bacteriophage susceptibility in clinical Enterococcus faecalis reflects host genomic background and Epa-associated phage adsorption
papers.abstract: Cytolysin-positive Enterococcus faecalis has been implicated as a disease-associated pathobiont in alcohol-associated hepatitis, motivating development of selective bacteriophage-based strategies. However, strain-level determinants of phage susceptibility remain incompletely understood. We characterized the host range of three E. faecalis phages, {Phi}Ef2.1, {Phi}Ef2.2, and {Phi}Ef2.3Ev, across 45 clinical isolates and investigated bacterial and phage factors associated with adsorption and productive infection. Isolates were characterized by whole-genome sequencing, cytolysin status, antimicrobial resistance determinants, and predicted anti-phage defense systems. Phage susceptibility was measured by efficiency of plating (EoP) and adsorption assays. Thirty-five of the 45 isolates (77.8%), including all 15 cylLs-positive isolates, were susceptible to at least one of the three phages at EoP [≥]0.01. {Phi}Ef2.1 and {Phi}Ef2.2 showed greater activity against cylLs-positive isolates, which also carried higher burdens of predicted antimicrobial resistance determinants and anti-phage defense system types. Analysis of 367 complete E. faecalis RefSeq genomes classified the variable region of the enterococcal polysaccharide antigen (epa) locus into 15 recurrent architecture groups that were associated with phage-specific adsorption patterns. Efficient adsorption did not always result in productive infection, indicating additional post-adsorption barriers. AbiD emerged as a candidate factor associated with reduced {Phi}Ef2.2 productivity, although this signal was prediction-tool dependent, while unexplained post-adsorption blocks suggest the involvement of additional uncharacterized mechanisms. These findings link naturally occurring epa architecture to phage adsorption and highlight distinct post-adsorption constraints on host range, providing a framework for rational phage selection against clinically relevant E. faecalis populations.

papers.title: Staphylococcus aureus enhances influenza A virus replication through modulation of host cell vesicular transport
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) is a major respiratory pathogen that causes substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide. A significant complication of primary IAV infection is secondary bacterial co-infection. Here, we report that Staphylococcus aureus enhances IAV replication through the activity of the surface protein fibronectin-binding protein A (FnbA). The pro-viral activity of FnbA is conserved across multiple IAV strains and is associated with reduced abundance of the host vesicular trafficking proteins VPS26A and VTA1. FnbA does not substantially increase viral protein abundance or alter intracellular distribution. Instead, pro-viral activity is associated with a greater proportion of infectious progeny particles and increased release of infectious virions from infected cells. Thus, we identify FnbA as a bacterial factor that enhances IAV replication and demonstrate that S. aureus can manipulate host cell processes to promote the production and release of infectious virus.

papers.title: Long terminal repeats influence deletion propensity and genome instability in proviruses across major retroviruses
papers.abstract: A hallmark of retroviral infection is integration of viral genomes into host chromosomes to form proviruses. Most proviruses are defective, particularly in people with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, with large internal deletions as a dominant outcome. The contribution of retroviral long terminal repeats (LTRs) in the formation of large internal deletions remains unclear. We used dual-fluorophore reporters based on HIV-1, HIV-2, and HTLV-1 LTRs, integrated at AAVS1 by CRISPR/Cas9, to test whether LTRs influence proviral integrity in the absence of reverse transcriptase or integrase. Cerulean expression was driven by the LTR and mCherry by an independent human promoter. Double-positive (Cerulean/mCherry) cells were a proxy for intact vectors, whereas single mCherry cells indicated latent and/or defective proviruses. Double-positive cells harboured intact vectors for all constructs. Non-inducible single mCherry populations were enriched for extensively deleted proviruses with HIV-1, HIV-2, or HTLV-1 LTRs, whereas the LTR-deficient reporter yielded few single mCherry cells, all with intact proviruses. The presence of LTRs was significantly associated with deleted genomes. HIV-1 and HTLV-1 showed higher observed deletion rates than HIV-2, but this was not statistically significant owing to limited sequence numbers. Single Cerulean populations across all constructs showed recurrent deletions affecting the mCherry cassette and upstream promoter, with short direct repeats at deletion junctions. These likely reflect microhomology-mediated end joining as a contributing repair mechanism during CRISPR/Cas9-mediated integration, in which LTRs may not directly contribute. Together, these data identify retroviral LTRs as contributors to the formation of large internal deletions in proviruses.

papers.title: Tropism of Drosophila innubila Nudivirus in Cell Culture and in Tissues
papers.abstract: Most viruses are successful because they can infect and exploit specific host tissues for reproduction and transmission. As a result, we often classify viruses by their ability to infect different tissues: respiratory, reproductive and gut, for example. Thus, knowing the tissue and cellular tropism of a virus may elucidate aspects of its biology including routes of transmission and virulence. We studied tropism of the Drosophila innubila Nudivirus (DiNV) in cells and infected hosts. DiNV is a nudivirus, a family of viruses related to the baculoviruses that are relatively large (150-200 nm), contain large double-stranded DNA genomes, and infect different host tissues. Cultured cells stained with an antibody against the DiNV nucleocapsid demonstrated punctate staining in the cytoplasm by confocal microscopy. Electron micrographs of infected cells, on the other hand demonstrated that virions are present in the nucleus. After purification, DiNV was often associated with multimembrane-like vesicles as described for Oryctes rhinoceros nudivirus. We examined tropism in hosts first by sagittal section and found most virus associated with the gut and, to a lesser extent, reproductive tissues. Upon dissection and electron microscopy, we found that DiNV in the gut is primarily in the visceral muscle of the gut and not the lumen as might be expected for a virus if transmitted fecal-orally.

papers.title: Allyl chloride respiration by Dehalobacter shapes the fate of 1,2,3-trichloropropane
papers.abstract: The synthetic compound 1,2,3-trichloropropane (1,2,3-TCP) is a persistent groundwater contaminant and probable human carcinogen for which effective detoxification pathways remain limited. Under anoxic conditions, microbial transformation of 1,2,3-TCP typically stalls at the intermediate allyl chloride, preventing complete detoxification. Here, we report the enrichment and characterization of Dehalobacter restrictus strain XRTCP, a bacterium capable of coupling dichloroelimination of 1,2,3-TCP with subsequent hydrogenolysis of allyl chloride to propene. While dichloroelimination to allyl chloride has been previously observed, the ability to utilize allyl chloride as a respiratory electron acceptor represents a previously unrecognized metabolic capability. This transformation was linked to microbial growth, with cell densities increasing by up to 74-fold during 1,2,3-TCP reduction and 15.8-fold during allyl chloride transformation. Metagenomic and metaproteomic analyses revealed a diverse repertoire of reductive dehalogenases (RDases), with expression patterns that differed between 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride amendments. Notably, a tcpA-like RDase was expressed under both 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride conditions, while distinct RDases were preferentially expressed under each substrate, indicating functional specialization within the dechlorination pathway. Despite this metabolic capability, propene formation remained limited due to rapid abiotic transformation of allyl chloride, primarily via reactions with reduced sulfur species, highlighting a critical branching point between biotic and abiotic pathways. These findings demonstrate that allyl chloride can function as a growth-supporting respiratory electron acceptor. More broadly, this work reveals how interactions between microbial metabolism and geochemical processes govern contaminant fate, with implications for improving both monitored natural attenuation and engineered bioremediation strategies for chlorinated solvents.

papers.title: Single-site DNA methylation activates retron defence by enabling effector tetramerisation
papers.abstract: Retrons are unique among bacterial defence systems in using DNA to sense phage infection. They achieve this by producing multicopy single-stranded DNA (msDNA) that monitors the activity of DNA-targeting phage proteins. Although we understand how extensive msDNA perturbations such as degradation activate retrons, activation by subtle chemical modifications remains enigmatic. Here, we used a structure-function approach to elucidate how single-site msDNA methylation activates Retron-Sen2. The cryo-EM structure of Retron-Sen2 features RcaT, the most prevalent retron effector, sequestered as an inactive dimer within a four-component assembly of previously undescribed architecture. Methylation by DNA adenine methyltransferase disrupts the RcaT-msDNA interaction and exposes a previously occluded interface that enables RcaT dimers to form tetramers, leading to retron disassembly. We show that RcaT dimer-dimer assembly is essential for its toxicity. To assess whether this is a conserved RcaT feature, we characterised additional homologues. RcaTs capable of tetramerisation or higher-order oligomerisation are toxic and form distinct phylogenetic clades from RcaTs that remain dimeric and are non-toxic. Together, our findings provide a paradigm for retron activation by single-site msDNA modifications and showcase how variation in an intrinsic protein property can diversify the toxicity of the same bacterial defence effector during evolution.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetics and Efficacy of the FimH Inhibitor Sibofimloc in Preventing Necrotizing Enterocolitis in Preterm Piglets
papers.abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a disease in preterm infants associated with an increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae. FimH, a mannose-binding adhesin on Enterobacteriaceae type 1 fimbriae, mediates mucosal attachment and TLR4-dependent inflammatory cascades. We evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of an oral FimH inhibitor (Sibofimloc) to reduce Enterobacteriaceae colonization and prevent NEC in preterm piglets. We performed a 9-d dose-escalation safety study (10, 25, 50 mg/kg BID) assessing absorption and tolerability and a 10-d randomized efficacy study. Piglets in the efficacy study received an infant formula diet with or without oral sibofimloc (40 mg/kg BID), or donor human milk (DHM) as a healthy control. NEC incidence, tissue histopathology, and gut microbiota composition via metagenomic whole-genome sequencing (WGS) were evaluated. Systemic exposure data reveal that sibofimloc was dose-dependently absorbed, while plasma levels decreased from postnatal day 2 to day 8, indicating reduced drug absorption with maturation of the intestinal barrier. Treatment with sibofimloc did not reduce NEC incidence (100% in sibofimloc in formula controls) or severity, whereas DHM-fed piglets experienced 0% NEC. Sibofimloc-treated animals exhibited significantly reduced crypt depths, demonstrating heightened mucosal injury and impaired regenerative capacity. WGS revealed that sibofimloc-treated animals maintained a gut luminal microbiota composition similar to untreated formula controls, dominated by Clostridium perfringens (C. perfringens). Selective targeting of FimH-expressing Enterobacteriaceae was insufficient to prevent NEC or alter the gut microbiota in this preterm piglet model, underscoring the complexity of NEC-associated microbial communities and suggesting that additional microbial targets and other colonization mechanisms may contribute to disease development.

papers.title: HSF1 inhibition potentiates the antifungal activity and proteome instability induced by the fungal Hsp110 inhibitor 2H
papers.abstract: Fungal infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide; however, therapeutic options are limited and are increasingly compromised by antifungal resistance. Heat Shock Protein 110 kDa (Hsp110) is an essential molecular chaperone required for protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and fungal viability and has recently emerged as a promising antifungal target. We previously identified 2H, a first-in-class inhibitor of fungal Hsp110 proteins that exhibits broad-spectrum antifungal activity through disruption of proteostasis. Heat Shock Transcription Factor 1 (HSF1), the master regulator of cellular stress responses and chaperone expression, has also been proposed as a potential antifungal target, although direct pharmacological evidence supporting this strategy remains limited. Here, we investigated the effects of combining the HSF1 inhibitor DTHIB with the fungal Hsp110 inhibitor 2H in Cryptococcus neoformans and Candida albicans. Although DTHIB alone exhibited minimal antifungal activity, it significantly enhanced the growth-inhibitory and fungicidal effects of 2H. Notably, this potentiating effect was specific to 2H and was not observed with fluconazole. Consistent with the roles of Hsp110 and HSF1 in proteostasis, 2H induced extensive accumulation of detergent-insoluble protein aggregates in C. neoformans, whereas HSF1 inhibition further increased both the abundance and diversity of aggregated proteins. Quantitative proteomic analyses demonstrated that 2H induces proteome-wide protein aggregation, impacting proteins involved in a broad range of essential cellular processes, with high-molecular-weight proteins exhibiting particular susceptibility. Together, these findings provide pharmacological evidence supporting HSF1 as a promising antifungal sensitization target and demonstrate the utility of 2H as a chemical probe for studying Hsp110-dependent proteostasis. Simultaneous disruption of both HSF1-mediated stress responses and Hsp110-dependent proteostasis promotes extensive proteome instability and enhances antifungal activity, highlighting a potential new strategy for antifungal drug development.

papers.title: HIV-1 envelope glycan loss links receptor adaptation and innate immune escape in SHIVs
papers.abstract: Simian-human immunodeficiency viruses (SHIVs) are widely used to model HIV-1 infection in macaques, yet most SHIVs encoding circulating HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins (Env) replicate poorly because of inefficient use of macaque CD4 and sensitivity to host antiviral responses. During adaptation to macaques, Env is therefore subject to multiple selective pressures to improve receptor utilization while maintaining function in the face of host immune restriction. Type I interferon (IFN) is a major component of the host antiviral response during acute infection, and IFN resistance increases during SHIV adaptation to macaques through serial passage. However, the viral determinants of this resistance have remained unclear. Here, we show that serial passage of a lineage of SHIVs in macaques selected Env variants with markedly increased resistance to IFN- and enhanced replication in macaque CD4+ T lymphocytes. IFN- resistance mapped principally to loss of two highly conserved N-linked glycans at N197 and N276 near the CD4-binding site. Glycan loss altered the conformational landscape of virus-associated Env, enhanced macaque CD4-dependent entry and membrane fusion without increasing human CD4-dependent entry, and reduced incorporation of the IFN-inducible restriction factors IFITM3 and IFITM3A into progeny virions. Depletion of IFITM3/3A rendered the parental SHIV highly resistant to IFN- and abolished differential IFN- sensitivity among parental, adapted, and glycan-loss viruses. These findings reveal that loss of receptor-proximal Env glycans can simultaneously improve utilization of a heterologous CD4 receptor and promote escape from IFN-mediated restriction, linking receptor adaptation and innate immune evasion during lentiviral adaptation to a new host.

papers.title: The mitochondrial transaminase GOT2 supports Japanese encephalitis virus replication in neuronal cells
papers.abstract: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is the leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia, yet the host pathways that sustain its replication in the central nervous system remain poorly defined, and no antiviral therapies exist. Here we combine time-resolved transcriptomics and proteomics in mouse neuroblastoma (Neuro-2a) cells with time-resolved proteomics of infected mouse brain, integrated using directionality-penalized p-value merging. JEV infection was accompanied by progressive induction of interferon-stimulated proteins and by changes in the abundance of enzymes of central carbon and energy metabolism, spanning the tricarboxylic acid cycle, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation and glutaminolysis. Temporal clustering of the brain proteome linked oxidative phosphorylation remodelling to a dependence on glutamine metabolism. Glutamine antagonism with DON reduced viral RNA, whereas glycolytic inhibition and AKT modulation did not significantly alter it under the conditions tested. Silencing of the mitochondrial transaminase GOT2 reduced JEV RNA, viral protein, and infectious virus production in human SH-SY5Y cells. Our findings identify a glutamine-GOT2 axis as a metabolic dependency of JEV and a candidate host-directed antiviral target.

papers.title: Excessive sample reagent incubation time increases the risk of false rifampin resistance results in Xpert(R) MTB/RIF Ultra tests performed on paucibacillary Mycobacterium tuberculosis sputum.
papers.abstract: A high rate of false rifampicin resistance (RIF-R) was recently reported in paucibacillary sputum samples tested with the Xpert(R) MTB/RIF Ultra (Ultra) assay. However, 96% of the studied facilities started the test 8 - 12 hours after addition of sample reagent (SR), exceeding the manufacturers recommended limit of 4 hours. Assessed whether excessive long SR incubation could lead to similar false RIF-R results in paucibacillary samples in a reference laboratory setting. We evaluated the performance of the Ultra assay following incubation of TB-negative sputum spiked with 300 CFU/mL and 100,000 CFU/mL levels of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) H37Rv in SR for different durations (15 min to 24hrs.) at different temperatures (-20 to 370C) to determine the effect on RIF result calls. No false RIF-R results were observed in these samples with 105 CFU/mL Mtb at any of the conditions tested, even when they deviated largely from recommended limits. Similarly, freezing the 300 CFU/mL SR treated samples at minus 200C for 18 h also prevented the development of false RIF-R results. However, sputum spiked with 300 CFU/ml Mtb, produced false RIF-R calls at longer incubation times and higher incubation temperatures than are recommended by the manufacturer. Approximately half of the results displayed melt patterns consistent with hetero-resistance, indicating SR-induced mutagenesis in a wild-type background. This study demonstrates that extended off-label SR incubation of paucibacillary specimens beyond the recommended 4-hour limit can generate false RIF-R results. Freezing paucibacillary specimens in SR may mitigate this risk although it is not yet an approved procedure.

papers.title: Disruption of cAMP Signalling and RNA Regulation Confers Cefiderocol Resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii
papers.abstract: Cefiderocol is a siderophore-conjugated cephalosporin used to treat severe multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections. Its recent prioritisation for US national preparedness underscores its clinical importance, yet resistance can emerge despite apparent in vitro susceptibility. Here, we identify two regulatory routes to cefiderocol resistance in carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB): mutation of the cAMP-producing adenylate cyclase CavA and truncation of the glycine-rich RNA-binding domain of the post-transcriptional regulator Hfq. These variants occurred in contemporary clinical isolates, conferred resistance in a murine CRAB lung-infection model and imposed minimal fitness costs. In Escherichia coli, deletion of the CavA orthologue cyaA increased competitive fitness during sub-inhibitory cefiderocol exposure. Hfq-CLASH and integrated omics revealed Hfq-dependent regulation of Fur-associated iron homeostasis in A. baumannii. Under iron limitation, truncated-Hfq induced a defence-primed state that attenuated siderophore uptake and reduced cefiderocol activity. These findings identify bacterial regulatory state and iron availability as determinants of cefiderocol susceptibility, with implications for resistance surveillance and susceptibility testing.

papers.title: Anti-trypanosomal activity and target validation of the M17 leucyl-aminopeptidase inhibitor DDD00057570 in Trypanosoma cruzi
papers.abstract: Background: Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, affects six to seven million people, and its treatment still relies on two drugs introduced more than fifty years ago, both of limited efficacy and poorly tolerated. The major acidic M17 leucyl-aminopeptidase of T. cruzi is expressed in all developmental stages of the parasite and has been proposed as a drug target, but it has not been pharmacologically validated. Methodology/Principal Findings: We assessed DDD00057570, a compound originally identified as an inhibitor of the orthologue enzyme of Leishmania major, against the recombinant T. cruzi enzyme and against the parasite. The compound inhibited the recombinant enzyme with an IC50 of 2.7 {+/-} 0.9 {micro}M and reduced the proliferation of insect-stage epimastigotes, with a half-maximal effective concentration of 3.7 {+/-} 1.1 {micro}M. Parasites engineered to overexpress the enzyme were twice as resistant to the compound as wild-type parasites, indicating that the enzyme is a primary target in the living parasite. Treatment increased the proportion of epimastigotes with fragmented DNA. In infected mammalian cells, the compound reduced the release of trypomastigotes, the stage responsible for dissemination in the mammalian host, with a half-maximal effective concentration of 1.3 {+/-} 0.6 {micro}M, while its half-maximal cytotoxic concentration on CHO-K1 mammalian host cells was 41.5 {+/-} 3.9 {micro}M, resulting in a selectivity index of approximately 32. Conclusions/Significance: These results validate the major M17 leucyl-aminopeptidase as a drug target in T. cruzi through target overexpression, and identify DDD00057570 as a selective lead structure warranting mechanistic, pharmacokinetic and in vivo studies toward a new treatment for Chagas disease.

papers.title: Reversible fixation of microbial cells for targeted genomics
papers.abstract: Phylogeny- or activity-based fluorescent labelling of microorganisms coupled with fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) is a powerful approach to rapidly isolate cells of interest from complex communities for targeted genomics. However, the method has not been widely adopted because standard paraformaldehyde or ethanol fixation procedures hamper nucleic acid recovery and/or long-term sample storage. Here, we present dithiobis(succinimidyl propionate) (DSP) as a reversible fixative for microbial cells that enables fluorescence imaging and DNA extraction and amplification for sequencing. DSP fixation is compatible with widely used fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) approaches and bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging, and can be applied to diverse sample types, where it consistently performed as well as paraformaldehyde. Furthermore, high-quality genomes were obtained from individual and multiple bacterial cells selectively extracted from complex samples using FISH-FACS. Thus, DSP is a dual-use fixative for microbiome imaging and sequencing, improving targeted microbial genomics.

papers.title: Viral dispersal drives changes in population composition
papers.abstract: In an acute viral infection, a small seeding population expands rapidly over several orders of magnitude, then declines. This vast population growth is accompanied by spatial expansion as infection spreads to new anatomical sites within the host. Evolutionary theory predicts that spatially expanding populations experience more extreme stochastic losses of genetic diversity than spatially unstructured populations. To test this prediction in the context of viral dynamics, we evaluated the impact of spatial expansion on viral population genetic structure and assessed how modulators of viral dispersal affected this structure. To this end, we developed a means of implementing the spatial expansion of influenza A virus in cell culture and applied it to a viral population carrying a diverse genetic barcode. Across this simplified cellular landscape, we found that spatial expansion produces a patchwork of distinct viral subpopulations. We then evaluated the consequences for population structure of two modulators of viral dispersal: extracellular viscosity and a common polymorphism in the viral attachment protein. Both physical constraint and viral phenotype altered the extent of genetic bottlenecking and spatial heterogeneity that developed during expansion, indicating that environmental features and viral traits that modulate dispersal also modulate viral population composition, diversity and evolution.

papers.title: Dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids interact with select gut microbes to produce bioactive metabolites found in infant gut metabolomes
papers.abstract: Gut microbes metabolize nutrients in infant diets, producing compounds that play roles in host health. Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) are an important component of infant diets, supporting neurological development and immune regulation. Emerging evidence demonstrates that gut microbes, alongside the host, participate in the metabolism of dietary lipids, highlighting an underexplored avenue for LCPUFA biology. In this work, alkyne-tagged eicosapentaenoic acid (EPAALK) was used to investigate interactions between LCPUFAs and the gut microbiota. Flow cytometry and comparative metabolomics identified gut microbial EPA interactors in the ileum of mice. Further comparative metabolomics analysis identified the conversion of EPA to N-acyl amino acids, including attachment to phenylalanine (EP-Phe) and leucine (EP-Leu). Targeted analysis of ex vivo stool cultures determined that EP-Phe and EP-Leu are produced by gut bacteria. A survey of lipid-relevant infant gut bacteria determined various flow cytometry-confirmed EPA-microbe interactions and identified Enterococcus faecalis, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, and Clostridium bifermentans as competent producers of EP-Phe or EP-Leu. Thus, both novel metabolites from diet-derived inputs and microbial producers of these metabolites were identified. Together, this highlights important microbiome-centric and mechanistic consequences of LCPUFA consumption and emphasizes that the gut microbiome may be an important consideration in targeted supplementation strategies.

papers.title: Evolutionary expansion of the bacterial ompW gene family enables functional diversification during host adaptation
papers.abstract: The outer membrane protein W (OmpW) family comprises minor porins essential for environmental adaptation and host interactions in Gram-negative bacteria. However, ompW is conventionally treated as a ubiquitous single-copy gene, masking its true evolutionary complexity. Through comprehensive phylogenetic analysis across thousands of reference genomes, we reveal that ompW is present in nearly half of Gram-negative lineages, exhibiting a patchy distribution governed by a birth-and-death model of evolution with recurrent duplications and horizontal transfer. Notably, copy number expansions concentrate in lineages associated with eukaryotic hosts, linking paralog accumulation to niche adaptation. Experimental validation in Acinetobacter baumannii reveals four distinct loci that maintain high structural conservation despite sequence divergence, yet undergo profound functional specialization spanning from baseline physiological maintenance to modulating host colonization and persistence in vitro and in vivo. These findings dismantle the single-copy paradigm, demonstrating that widespread gene family expansion and paralog diversification drive the phenotypic plasticity required for bacteria to colonize hostile host environments.

papers.title: Five decades of human H1N1 evolution reveal conserved glycan receptor specificity
papers.abstract: H1N1 influenza viruses have circulated continuously among human populations for five decades. During evolution, the hemagglutinin has accumulated amino acid substitutions in and around the receptor-binding site (RBS), mainly due to antigenic pressure, potentially altering receptor recognition and binding profiles. Here, we investigated the glycan-binding properties of H1N1 strains collected from 1977 through 2024 using ELISA, flow cytometry, and tissue histochemistry to characterize changes in receptor-binding specificity over time. Across the strains examined, we observe a recurring preference for binding 2,6-sialylated di-LacNAc N-glycans. Binding to 2,3-sialylated glycans was generally undetectable, although A/Hongkong/117/1977 and A/New Caledonia/20/1999 bind chicken tracheal tissues. Interestingly, post-pandemic H1N1 viruses fluctuate in their relative binding avidities. The responsible amino acids, in turn, have different effects in pre-pandemic HA proteins. We also report a classical egg-adapted H1N1 mutant that shows null binding across platforms. These findings highlight the contribution of RBS mutations during initial adaptation and evolution of human H1N1 influenza viruses to glycan-binding properties, which, in contrast to H3N2 viruses, never fail to bind glycans that correlate with avian erythrocyte hemagglutination.

papers.title: Gain-of-function mutations in the RodZ juxtamembrane domain promote Rod system activity in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: The peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall protects bacteria from osmotic lysis and determines their shape. In rod-shaped bacteria, the lateral wall is elongated by the Rod system (elongasome). This synthetic machine is built around the RodA-PBP2 PG synthase complex, the actin-like protein MreB, and the accessory proteins MreC, MreD, and RodZ. Notably, RodZ shares a similar domain organization with FtsN, an essential division protein that triggers PG synthesis by the division apparatus (divisome). Both are single pass transmembrane proteins that bind actin-like proteins in the cytoplasm and have largely unstructured periplasmic regions capped by small, folded C-terminal domains. We therefore investigated whether RodZ might function like FtsN in activating the Rod system. To this end, gain-of-function variants of Escherichia coli RodZ were isolated that restored growth and shape to cells producing a hypomorphic mreC mutant. Production of these RodZ variants in wild-type cells increased resistance to the MreB antagonist A22 and enhanced sensitivity to the beta-lactam mecillinam. These phenotypes have all previously been associated with Rod system hyperactivation, and we found that they were caused by substitutions in the cytoplasmic juxtamembrane (JM) domain of RodZ. This domain is analogous to the N-terminus of FtsN known to promote divisome activation via its interaction with filaments of the actin-like FtsA protein. Structural modeling indicates that the JM domain of RodZ is similarly likely to associate with MreB filaments. Our results therefore support a model in which RodZ activates PG synthesis by the Rod system via a mechanism analogous to divisome activation by FtsN.

papers.title: Murine cytomegalovirus m119-118 encodes a new viral Fc receptor antagonizing host Fc receptor activation
papers.abstract: Cytomegaloviruses (CMVs) encode numerous immunomodulatory proteins to counteract innate and adaptive immunity. One class of immune evasion proteins is viral Fc receptors (vFcRs), which bind to the Fc region of IgG antibodies and interfere with antibody-mediated effector functions crucial for antiviral defense. Despite the established role of vFcRs in modulating antibody-mediated immunity, their contribution to viral pathogenesis in vivo remains incompletely understood. Although human CMV (HCMV) encodes four vFcRs, only a single vFcR, fcr-1 encoded by gene m138, has been identified in murine CMV (MCMV). By comparing and cloning the genomes of MCMV strains v70, K181+, and K181Perth, we identified a frameshift mutation affecting the spliced m119-118 transcript in K181Perth. This finding prompted us to investigate the function of the m119-118 gene. We show that it encodes a second MCMV vFcR, which we named fcr-2. It is structurally similar to its positional homolog in HCMV, UL119-118/gp68, and binds specifically to the Fc part of murine IgG. Deletion of both vFcRs genes from the MCMV genome resulted in substantially reduced Fc-binding to the surface of infected cells, indicating a complementary function of the vFcRs. Functional assays with viral deletion mutants further demonstrated that both proteins inhibit host Fc receptor activation in a cooperative fashion. Although an m119-118-deficient MCMV was only marginally attenuated in infected BALB/c mice, an m119-118 and m138 double mutant attained significantly lower organ titers than the m138-deficient mutant. These data suggest an important cooperative function of the two MCMV vFcRs for viral dissemination and pathogenesis in vivo.

papers.title: Exploring the antibiotic-producing capabilities of Canadian High Arctic bacteria
papers.abstract: Microbial communities in harsh environments such as the Canadian high Arctic, remain a relatively unexplored source of antimicrobial natural products. In this study, we developed a pipeline for screening and evaluating bacterial isolates cultured from 23 Canadian high Arctic soil, sediment, and active-layer permafrost samples to discover antibacterial compounds. The pipeline incorporated an undergraduate studentsourcing program and produced created a collection of over 350 bacterial isolates with preliminary antibacterial activity. Following dereplication, whole genome sequencing and secondary screening by co-culture assays, five isolates were prioritized to test crude extracts for antibacterial activity. Among bioactive crude extracts from these isolates, the Pseudomonas isolate with the most potent activity against S. aureus was analyzed. Using liquid chromatography bioactivity guided fractionation, we identified a potential bioactive compound known as koreenceine A, a compound previously only isolated from a Pseudomonas from temperate soil and involved in gene expression of other their microbial community. Here we expanded the known antibiotic activity of koreenceine A and confirmed that a {triangleup}kecBCD genetic knockout of the putative biosynthetic gene cluster significantly abrogated the antibacterial activity.

papers.title: A Third-generation Lentiviral Vector System for Flow Virometry-based Analysis of HIV-1 Env and Other Viral Envelope Proteins
papers.abstract: Individual human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) particles can differ in their envelope protein (Env) despite being genetically identical. This non-genetic diversity can influence antibody recognition and has been implicated in the formation of persistent virus fractions that escape complete inhibition by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Investigating non-genetic diversity in HIV and other viruses requires approaches capable of characterizing antibody binding to individual viral particles. Flow virometry provides a promising tool for single-particle analysis, but a system combining high biosafety with specific particle labeling and versatility is lacking. Here, we developed a third-generation lentiviral vector system specifically designed for flow virometry. Fluorescent proteins were incorporated into the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein between the matrix- and capsid-encoding regions, flanked by viral protease cleavage sites, creating the packaging constructs pLentiFlow-eGFP and pLentiFlow-mCherry. Lentiviral particles (LVPs) based on pLentiFlow vectors were fluorescent and retained infectivity comparable to LVPs generated with the parental vector system despite reduced particle production. We optimized LVP detection on a CytoFLEX nano and defined a linear p24-based concentration range for reliable single-particle analysis. Using complementary controls, we demonstrated that background from the assessed sources accounted for no more than approximately 3% of events within a broad eGFP+ gate and confirmed that the detected fluorescent particles were predominantly membrane-enclosed. As a proof of concept, LVPs were pseudotyped with vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 spike, or HIV-1 Env. Envelope-specific antibody binding was detected using 8G5F11, CR3022 or PGT128, respectively, demonstrating that different viral surface proteins can be analyzed on a common particle backbone. Together, these results establish a third-generation lentiviral vector system for flow virometry that combines intrinsic particle labeling with high biosafety and flexible pseudotyping. The system provides a platform for investigating envelope protein-associated non-genetic diversity and its consequences for antibody recognition in HIV and other viruses.

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.
